These are words you use to talk about social issues and beliefs.
Should and Shall to Request Confirmation
You use the modals should and shall in questions that need confirmation. In these types of sentences, should and shall have very similar meanings.

For example:
Who shall I contact on your behalf?
When should I check in?

You can use should or shall in offers or requests.

For example:
Should I call the concierge for you?
Shall we dance?
Sometimes should and shall can have very different meanings. In these cases, context is especially important.

Compare these examples:
I shall contact him next week. (shall means intention)
I should contact him next week, but I'm nervous. (should means ought to)
Should I give money to some group?
Shall I donate money or time somewhere?
Should I obey all the laws?
Should I always cast my vote?
How should I find the best way to be civically responsible?
Will and Would for Willingness and Intention
You usually use will and won't to talk about the future. However, you can use them to express willingness (or unwillingness).
Talking about the present: will, won't
You can use will to talk about someone's willingness in the present moment to do something.

For example:
Sarah is the best - she will always help a friend in need.
You can use won't to talk about someone's unwillingness in the present moment to do something.

For example:
My brother won't text me back - he's angry with me.
You can use would or wouldn't to express willingness about the past as well.
When talking about the past, you can use would to express that someone was usually willing to do things.

For example:
Sarah was a kind person - she would always help a friend in need.
You use would to talk about usual situations in the past - not one time situations. However, you can use wouldn't to talk about unwillingness in the past for all kinds of situations.

For example:
My brother wouldn't vacuum the house, but he would wash the car.
My sister wouldn't stop talking so I didn't make my class on time.

images.text:
Civic Responsibility
You often hear people talking about their civic responsibility. It sounds important! What does it mean? Very simply, “civic responsibility” means responsibility of a citizen. I would like to be a responsible citizen. Should I give more money to some group? Shall I donate money or time somewhere? How should I find the best way to be civically responsible? I did some research to find out and I will share what I learned with you.

The importance of civic responsibility is paramount to the success of democracy and philanthropy. By engaging in civic responsibility, citizens ensure and uphold certain democratic values. Civic responsibility differs from civic duty, which consists of actions that are legally required of citizens. Examples of civic duty in the U.S. are paying taxes, registering for the draft, attending school and serving on juries. The most common form of civic responsibility is volunteering. There are many ways to help the community by volunteering time and I will make a point of volunteering as much as I can. Most people I know would volunteer time around the holidays. What are some other ways to be responsible? Voting is not mandatory in the U.S. Should I always cast my vote? Yes!

Voting is a way to be a responsible citizen. Should I obey all the laws? Yes! Not just to avoid punishment, but because obeying laws and behaving in an ethical manner is a civic responsibility. Should I make charitable donations when and if I am able? Yes! Those people who are in a position to give financial support to others should always do so. I remember my parents would make donations to several charities every year and it was a good lesson for me, as a child. I learned that there are people that have much less than we did, and that it was important for us to help other people. I will continue what my parents started and try to contribute as much as I can for the good of the whole community.

contents.value: Though it isn't officially mandatory, civic responsibility is a duty everyone has. We abide by the law. Because we live in a democracy, we have choices and we exercise the right to make them. Some of us are more generous than others; most philanthropy comes from those who have an appreciation for life and liberty. Those people are not always wealthy. Some of the most philanthropic people have next to nothing.
